name: Amiodarone
class: Antiarrhythmic (class III with multi-channel and beta-blocking effects)
summary: The most effective antiarrhythmic across atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, at the price of a distinctive, slowly developing multi-organ toxicity profile and an enormous half-life.
mechanism: Blocks cardiac potassium (IKr), sodium, and L-type calcium channels plus noncompetitive beta-adrenergic blockade, prolonging action potential duration and refractoriness in all cardiac tissue.
pharmacodynamics: Class III-dominant antiarrhythmic; prolongs QT, slows sinus rate and AV conduction.

pharmacokinetics.onset: IV: minutes to hours; oral: days to weeks
pharmacokinetics.duration: Weeks to months after discontinuation (tissue accumulation)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4, CYP2C8) to active metabolite desethylamiodarone

dosing.adult: Ventricular arrhythmias: oral loading 800–1600 mg/day for 1–3 weeks, then maintenance 100–400 mg/day; VF/pulseless VT arrest: IV 300 mg bolus (may repeat 150 mg)

safety.pregnancy: Avoid — crosses placenta; fetal hypothyroidism and goiter (contains iodine)
contraindications: Marked sinus bradycardia or high-grade AV block without pacemaker
warnings: QT prolongation / proarrhythmia (especially with other QT-prolonging drugs)
monitoring: Baseline and periodic chest imaging and pulmonary function
Thyroid function tests (baseline, then every 6 months)
safety.overdose: Supportive care; bradycardia/asystole treated with pacing and inotropes

indications: Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias refractory to other agents
clinicalPearls: Effects and toxicity persist for months after stopping due to the enormous half-life.
Screen for pulmonary and thyroid toxicity at baseline and periodically during therapy.
good: Refractory or life-threatening arrhythmias when other agents fail.
bad: Young patients, pregnancy, or long-term use without structured toxicity surveillance.
